title: July 2026: thesis more validated — hires break to a new cycle low as U-3 falls on exits
html:
Verdict: MORE validated. The hiring side broke to a fresh cycle low while every firing gauge stayed benign, and U-3 fell for exactly the wrong reason — people leaving the labor force, not people finding work.

Since the June turn: The hires rate broke down from 3.4% to 3.2%, a new cycle low, with the level falling 278K to 5.05M — professional and business services alone shed 188K of hires and the finance-and-insurance hires rate collapsed from 1.9% to 1.4%. Quits eased 2.0% → 1.9% (3.1M). Against that, layoffs and discharges fell 1.1% → 1.0% (1.7M) and initial claims ran 203K in the week ended Aug 22 (4-wk avg 205,500) versus 229K a year earlier, with continuing claims at 1.778M against 1.942M a year ago and the insured rate pinned at 1.2%. Continuing/initial is ~8.8×. Openings rose to 7.27M (4.3% → 4.4%) and V/U pushed up to ~1.05 from ~1.01 — but June was revised down 177K to 7.18M, so the gain is against a lowered base, and the one real add was durable-goods manufacturing (+76K), a sector the benchmark revision just marked down 67K. Openings that don't convert into hires are the point, not a rebuttal. On the household side U-3 fell 4.2% → 4.1% and the unemployed count dropped 178K — yet employment fell 87K, the labor force shrank 264K, and 381K moved to not-in-labor-force. Participation slipped again to 61.4% (−0.7pp since January) and the employment-population ratio to 58.9%. U-6 held at 7.9%, so the U-6−U-3 gap widened to 3.8pp. Marginally attached rose 45K to 1.81M; part-time for economic reasons rose 123K to 4.80M. Payrolls printed −23K, with May and June revised down a combined 103K — June's +57K is now +20K — leaving the three-month average near 20K, below any plausible breakeven.

Contrarian wrinkles — and why they don't overturn it. Two data points cut against the thesis this month. First, every duration measure improved: mean duration 25.5 → 24.9 weeks, median 11.0 → 10.5, and the long-term unemployed fell 166K to 1.77M, dropping the 27-weeks-plus share from a four-year-high 27.3% to 25.5%. But the distribution underneath is less friendly than the headline: under-5-weeks fell 222K while 5–14 weeks (+113K) and 15–26 weeks (+105K) both rose, and the share unemployed 15 weeks or longer was essentially unchanged at 42.2%. The tail thinned; the stuck-in-the-middle cohort grew. With 381K exiting the labor force and marginally attached rising, the more likely reading is long-duration jobseekers giving up rather than getting hired — which is the head-fake, not a refutation of it. Second, prime-age EPOP ticked up 0.2pp to 80.4% (prime-age men 85.7% → 85.8%, still 0.8pp below May), retracing part of June's plunge — so June was partly noise, and this tracker should mark that down honestly. A third wrinkle sits on the firing side: workers on temporary layoff jumped 153K to 921K, though permanent job losers were little changed at 1.7M and the surge is hard to separate from the local-government-education seasonal quirk that drove the payroll miss.

Other notable: the Aug 28 preliminary benchmark revision put March 2026 nonfarm employment 79K (−0.1%) below the published level — far smaller than last year's −898K, so the establishment survey is no longer overstating the level the way it was. The composition matters more than the total: private payrolls −178K against government +99K, with retail trade −154.6K, private education and health −96K, wholesale trade −86.2K (−1.4%, the largest percentage cut), professional and business services −76K and manufacturing −67K, offset by transportation and warehousing +135.1K and information +87K. In the July payroll detail, financial activities fell another 14K and is now down 121K from its May 2025 peak, and health care — the sector carrying essentially all net job growth — added 22K against a 36K twelve-month average. Wage growth corroborates slack without layoffs: average hourly earnings +3.2% y/y, roughly 2.5% annualized over three months, against faster inflation. Falsification still requires a claims and layoff-rate spike; claims are running below year-ago levels, so there is none.

Sources: BLS JOLTS — July (rel. Sep 1), BLS Employment Situation — July (rel. Aug 7), BLS CES preliminary benchmark revision (rel. Aug 28), DOL weekly claims (rel. Aug 27). Next turn: August JOLTS, scheduled Sep 29 (August Employment Situation, Sep 4).

title: June 2026: thesis more validated — the head-fake phase is live
html:
Verdict: MORE validated. Every element of the fingerprint is present, and the damage is now migrating from the headline rate into participation — exactly the head-fake this tracker warns about.

Since the May turn: Hires rate stuck at 3.4% (cycle lows) and openings fell 7.59M → 7.36M (rate 4.6% → 4.4%), while layoffs held at 1.1% and initial claims sat near 2026 lows (~197K; 4-wk avg ~203K) — nobody is firing, nobody is hiring. Quits rate stayed low at 2.0%, though the level rose to 3.23M, a one-year high — a contrarian wrinkle worth watching. U-3 ticked down 4.3% → 4.2%, but entirely because participation fell 0.3pp to 61.5% (lowest since Mar 2021); prime-age EPOP dropped 0.6pp to 80.2%, the lowest since Dec 2022 (prime-age men −0.9pp to 85.7%). Long-term unemployed reached 1.9M — 27.3% of all unemployed, a four-year high — with mean duration at 25.5 weeks. Continuing claims (~1.78M) against initial (~197K) ≈ 9×: flat inflows, slow outflows — the newly unemployed can't get rehired.

Notable: the openings decline was concentrated in health care & social assistance (−147K) — the last reliable hiring engine cooling — plus leisure & hospitality (−86K) and wholesale trade (−74K); transportation/warehousing/utilities added +97K. Payrolls +57K in June confirm hiring, not firing, is the weak link. Falsification would require a claims/layoff spike; there is no sign of one.

Sources: BLS JOLTS (rel. Aug 4), BLS Employment Situation — June (rel. Jul 2), DOL weekly claims (rel. Jul 30). Next turn: July JOLTS, expected early September.
